{{Short description|Property of algebraic varieties and complex manifolds}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''geometric genus''' is a basic [[birational invariant]] {{math|''p''{{sub|''g''}}}} of [[algebraic varieties]] and [[complex manifold]]s.

==Definition==

The geometric genus can be defined for [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|non-singular]] complex projective varieties and more generally for [[complex manifold]]s of dimension {{math|''n''}} as the [[Hodge number]] {{math|''h''{{sup|''n'',0}}}}  (equal to {{math|''h''{{sup|0,''n''}}}} by [[Serre duality]]), that is, the dimension of the [[Canonical bundle#General case|canonical linear system]] plus one.

In other words, for a variety {{mvar|V}} of [[complex dimension]] {{mvar|n}} it is the number of linearly independent holomorphic {{mvar|n}}-[[differential form|forms]] to be found on {{mvar|V}}.<ref>Danilov & Shokurov (1998), [{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=mU6ciaFCC1IC|page=53|text=geometric genus}} p. 53]</ref> This definition, as the dimension of

:{{math|''H''{{sup|0}}(''V'',&Omega;{{sup|''n''}})}}

then carries over to any base [[field (mathematics)|field]], when {{math|&Omega;}} is taken to be the sheaf of [[Kähler differential]]s and the power is the (top) [[exterior power]], the [[canonical bundle|canonical line bundle]].

The geometric genus is the first invariant {{math|''p''{{sub|''g''}} {{=}} ''P''{{sub|1}}}} of a sequence of invariants {{math|''P''{{sub|''n''}}}} called the [[plurigenera]].

==Case of curves==

In the case of complex varieties, (the complex loci of) non-singular curves are [[Riemann surfaces]]. The algebraic definition of genus agrees with the [[Genus (mathematics)#Orientable surface|topological notion]]. On a nonsingular curve, the canonical line bundle has degree {{math|2''g''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2}}.

The notion of genus features prominently in the statement of the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]] (see also [[Riemann–Roch theorem for algebraic curves]]) and of the [[Riemann–Hurwitz formula]]. By the Riemann-Roch theorem, an irreducible plane curve of degree ''d'' has geometric genus

:<math>g=\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}-s,</math>

where ''s'' is the number of singularities when properly counted.

If {{mvar|C}} is an irreducible (and smooth) hypersurface in the [[Algebraic geometry of projective spaces|projective plane]] cut out by a polynomial equation of degree {{mvar|d}}, then its normal line bundle is the [[Serre twisting sheaf]] {{tmath|\mathcal O}}{{math|(''d'')}}, so by the [[adjunction formula]], the canonical line bundle of {{mvar|C}} is given by

: <math> \mathcal K_C = \left[ \mathcal K_{\mathbb P^2} + \mathcal O(d) \right]_{\vert C} = \mathcal O(d-3)_{\vert C} </math>

==Genus of singular varieties==

The definition of geometric genus is carried over classically to singular curves {{mvar|C}}, by decreeing that

:{{math|''p''{{sub|''g''}}(''C'')}}

is the geometric genus of the [[Normal scheme#The normalization|normalization]] {{math|''C''&prime;}}. That is, since the mapping

:{{math|''C''&prime; &rarr; ''C''}}

is [[birational]], the definition is extended by birational invariance.
